title: A policy flowing down the hierarchy
summary: A rule set at the top applies to every project below.

steps.n: The admin sets an organization policy that blocks service account key creation.
Every folder under the organization receives the constraint automatically.
The production project inherits it, so nobody there can create keys.
A developer runs the create key command in the project.
The call fails with an organization policy error that names the constraint.
The admin may allow an exception for one sandbox folder only, and it is recorded.

title: Choosing the right project for a command
summary: A named configuration decides which project receives the command.

steps.n: The engineer types gcloud compute instances list.
gcloud reads the active configuration for the account, project and region.
The configuration says acme-pay-dev, so the command targets dev.
gcloud sends the request using the engineer's credentials.
The API verifies the engineer has permission in that project and returns the list.
For production the engineer passes --project so the target is stated in the command.

title: A packet through firewall rules
summary: Implied deny and priority decide whether traffic is allowed.

steps.n: A client sends HTTPS to the load balancer's public address.
The load balancer sends the request to a VM on port 8080 from a Google range.
Rules are checked by priority and the lowest number that matches decides.
A rule allows tcp:8080 from the load balancer ranges to the web service account.
The VM sends its response back through the same path.
A direct connection from the internet to port 22 matches no allow rule and is dropped.

title: Autoscaling and autohealing in a MIG
summary: The group adds capacity under load and replaces a failing VM.

steps.n: CPU across the group climbs above the 60 percent target.
The autoscaler asks the group to add instances up to the maximum.
The group creates VMs from the template in several zones.
The health check marks one VM unhealthy after repeated failures.
The group deletes that VM and creates a fresh one from the template.
When load falls the autoscaler removes extra instances after a cooldown.

title: An object through its lifecycle
summary: Lifecycle rules move data to colder classes and then delete it.

steps.n: The application writes an export file to a Standard class bucket.
For the first weeks the file is read daily at Standard prices.
A lifecycle rule changes the storage class to Nearline.
Another rule moves the file to Archive for the cheapest keeping cost.
A final rule deletes the object, as required by the retention policy.
If someone overwrites the file, versioning keeps the previous version until it expires.

title: A pod using Workload Identity
summary: The pod gets short-lived Google credentials without any key file.

steps.n: The pod runs with a Kubernetes service account that is annotated with a Google service account.
The client library calls the GKE metadata server for credentials.
The metadata server checks the Kubernetes service account and its binding.
A token for the Google service account is returned and expires within the hour.
The pod calls Cloud Storage with the token.
IAM sees the Google service account has the bucket role and returns the data.

title: A request scaling Cloud Run
summary: Instances start on demand and stop when there is no traffic.

steps.n: No instance is running, so the platform starts one from the container image.
The container starts and listens on the port, which adds a short delay.
The instance handles the request and reads from the database.
The reply goes back to the client.
Concurrency fills, so more instances are added up to the maximum.
After the idle period the extra instances are removed and cost stops.

title: Cloud SQL failover
summary: The standby takes over when the primary zone fails.

steps.n: The application writes to the primary instance in zone A.
Every committed change is copied to the standby in zone B.
Zone A becomes unavailable and the primary stops answering.
The standby is promoted to primary, usually in about a minute.
The application reconnects to the same address and resumes writing.
Automated backups and point-in-time logs keep running for recovery.

title: Ack deadline and redelivery
summary: A message handled too slowly is delivered again.

steps.n: The publisher sends a message to the topic.
The subscription pushes it to the subscriber with a 10 second ack deadline.
The handler needs 45 seconds because it calls a slow service.
The deadline passes with no ack, so Pub/Sub delivers the message again.
The handler detects the id was already processed and skips the effect.
If the message still fails it goes to the dead-letter topic for review.

title: A burn rate alert
summary: The alert fires when the error budget is used too quickly.

steps.n: The service reports request counts and latencies to Cloud Monitoring.
Monitoring divides good requests by all requests over a window.
The objective is 99.9 percent, and the current error rate is far above the allowed 0.1 percent.
The budget would be gone in a few hours, so the on-call engineer is paged.
The engineer follows traces and logs to the failing release.
The release is reverted and the burn rate falls back to normal.

title: Terraform in CI with federation
summary: A pipeline plans and applies using a short-lived service account.

steps.n: The CI job exchanges its OIDC token with workload identity federation.
The federation grants permission to impersonate the Terraform service account.
Terraform locks the state object in the Cloud Storage bucket.
The plan compares the state with the real resources and shows changes.
After a reviewer approves, the apply runs with the same short-lived identity.
The new state is written, the old version is kept by versioning and the lock is released.

title: Failure and recovery: permission denied
summary: The exact missing permission is found instead of granting Owner.

steps.n: The developer reads an object and receives PERMISSION_DENIED for storage.objects.get.
The developer asks the admin to fix it, and the quick answer is to grant Owner.
The admin checks the principal, resource and permission in Policy Troubleshooter.
It shows that no binding on the bucket includes the needed permission.
The admin grants the object viewer role on that single bucket only.
The developer repeats the call and it succeeds.
The change is recorded, and IAM Recommender later removes any unused extras.
The project stays free of broad roles and the audit log shows a clean reason for the grant.

title: Failure and recovery: pods stuck pending
summary: A pool limit blocks scheduling until capacity is raised.

steps.n: The deployer scales a service from 3 to 20 pods.
The scheduler cannot place the pods and marks them Pending with Insufficient cpu.
The cluster autoscaler is asked to add nodes to the pool.
The node pool is already at its maximum of 3 nodes, so it cannot add more.
The operator describes a pod and reads the scheduling event and the autoscaler message.
The operator raises the node pool maximum and checks the project quota.
New nodes join and the scheduler places the waiting pods.
The team also lowers oversized requests so pods use capacity more efficiently.
